what: The later looks, on 2026-11-21, at the code for a full run on Spot machines that resumes after Google takes a machine back (cloud/gcp/pilot_local.sh, cloud/gcp/full_guest.sh, scripts/spot_checkpoint.sh and the three local tests), each after the changes the look before it had led to; the first review is spot_resume_review.json. Every look was by fresh AI agents told to refute the fixes, read-only on the repository; none ran anything in the cloud, and no run has been made. Criticism of code, not a result. Line numbers are those of the draft each agent read. 'what_was_done' under each finding is the lead agent's one-line account, not the verifier's.
the_shape_of_it: No look graded anything a blocker. The findings narrowed from the design (what may cross between machines, what the ledger must survive) to the edges of the rehearsal's own reporting and of two commands run in the same seconds. The guest and the checkpoint helper had no major finding from the third look on.
what_no_look_could_show: docs/cloud-notes.md, section 10.6: everything that needs a real machine, a real reclaim and a real bucket.

verifiers.subject: the launcher (cloud/gcp/pilot_local.sh) and its test
verifiers.summary: All of A1-A14 and the launcher side of K1-K6 are done as FIXES.md asks. I confirmed each by reading the code at the lines cited. The test passes on a default macOS TMPDIR: I ran `/bin/bash scripts/dev/test_spot_launcher.sh` myself and its last lines were "PASS old_mode_full-rehearsal / PASS old_mode_full / PASS old_full_edges / PASS spot_vm_matches_on_demand / 47 passed, 0 failed", exit 0. The four old modes match HEAD. The only change to code they run is the atomic close_run, plus refusals that apply only when a Spot state exists. I found no blocker. Against the five claims: (1) the cap arithmetic holds as long as the guest keeps the parts under the limit, though the inputs downloaded out of region are not counted. (2) and (4) fail in two narrow ways. A power loss of the Mac within seconds of a create can leave a VM with no ledger row, because neither the row append nor the state is flushed to disk. On the all-zones-refused path, the row is closed at zero without checking for leftover disks. (3) holds in normal use, but taking over a stale lock has a check-then-act race, which I reproduced with an injected 1 s delay. A pid reused after a reboot gives a refusal that tells the owner to kill an unrelated process. Two new problems come from the fix round. The rehearsal's record of which cuts were actually done (CUTS_DONE) is deleted with the state at the end and never printed, so a rehearsal can finish without one of its cuts and nobody is told. The 5-minute "not listed yet" guard is timed from when the row was opened, not from the create that went unclear. Smaller ones: the 90 % parts rule is reported as a cap shortage, and every guest PAUSED (including the new non-deadline pauses) starts another paid attempt.
verifiers.tests_run: `/bin/bash scripts/dev/test_spot_launcher.sh` with the default macOS TMPDIR, in the background; log at <SCRATCH>/spotdesign/rev3A/test.log. Last lines: "PASS old_mode_full-rehearsal", "PASS old_mode_full", "PASS old_full_edges", "PASS spot_vm_matches_on_demand", "47 passed, 0 failed", exit 0, finishing within the 15-minute budget. In scratch I also ran: (a) a bash 3.2 check that the EXIT trap runs on INT, TERM and HUP (it does, so the lock is released); (b) a stale-lock takeover race using spot_lock pulled from the script: 0 doubled holders in 40 trials of three concurrent takers, but 2 holders once a 1 s delay is put after the pid read (rev3A/lockt2.sh), which confirms the check-then-act window. No gcloud, no lake, no state-changing git; config.env was not read.

findings.line: 321-329 (row append and state saves before create), 136-139 (spot_save), 85-90 (close_run)
findings.title: A power loss of the Mac just after a create can leave a VM with no ledger row and no state naming it
findings.detail: Sequence: (1) spot_start appends attempt N's row with `printf >> $LEDGER` (line 321). (2) It saves the state with ATTEMPT=N (lines 322 and 325, write a temp file then mv). (3) It sends the create (line 329). Neither the row nor the state is fsynced. On macOS the writes stay in the buffer cache for up to tens of seconds, and os.fsync alone does not flush the drive's cache (F_FULLFSYNC does). If the Mac loses power in that window, both files can come back as they were before the start: no row, ATTEMPT=N-1, ACCOUNTED=N-1, LEDGER_ROWS at the old count. The LEDGER_ROWS backstop then sees nothing wrong. The next `watch` finds no open row and ACCOUNTED equal to ATTEMPT, and goes to spot_start. If the VM is still listed, spot_start dies and teardown purges it with no row. If Google has meanwhile reclaimed and deleted it, a new attempt starts. Either way that VM's time, up to MAXRUN (151200 s, about $50 at 1.20/h), is never recorded, so actual spend can pass the cap by one attempt. This breaks claims (2) and (4) for power loss; the window is small but real.
findings.fix: Make the row append durable before the create: append through python (open 'a', write, flush, os.fsync, and fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC) on Darwin), and fsync the directory. Write spot_save's temp file through a python helper that does the same before the rename. Apply F_FULLFSYNC in close_run and spot_ledger_zone too. Order: ledger durable, then state durable, then create.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the ledger row and the state naming the attempt are forced to disk (F_FULLFSYNC on macOS) before any create is sent; later also the state that announces the row.

findings.title: What the rehearsal actually cut is deleted at the end and never reported, so a missed or fallen-back cut goes unnoticed
findings.detail: A7 records in CUTS_DONE what each cut really did (for example `c3:reset>delete`). Nothing ever prints CUTS_DONE or saves it outside the state file. spot_finish runs `rm -f "$STATE"` first. The only trace is the transient line "rehearsal cut X in attempt N" in the watch terminal. Sequence: in full-spot-rehearsal the c3 gate needs state.json results_saved above RESULTS_SAVED. If the guest never saves a confirmed result while c3 is RUNNING (short c3, or confirms failing), the c3:reset cut never fires. Or a reset is refused and falls back to delete. The run ends DONE, the state is deleted, and the summary looks like a full rehearsal. Restoring saved replay results after a cut with no notice was never exercised, and nobody is told. Per the brief, a rehearsal that does not exercise what it claims is major.
findings.fix: In spot_finish (and spot_pause/abandon in rehearsal mode), before removing the state, print CUTS against CUTS_DONE, one line per configured cut: done / done by fallback / NOT DONE. Also write that list to $OUT/$RUNTAG/cuts.txt so the mirror and the results folder carry it. Consider ending a rehearsal with a non-zero status when a configured cut was not done.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: every configured cut is reported (done as configured, done by fallback, NOT DONE), the report is kept in cuts.txt, and a rehearsal that missed a cut ends with exit status 4.

findings.title: The 'not listed yet' guard is timed from when the row was opened, not from the create that went unclear
findings.detail: CREATED is the time the row was opened, before the first zone's create. Zone refusals can each take a minute or more, and spot_create_unclear adds 30 s. So the unclear create in zone 3 or 4 is sent 3 to 5 minutes after CREATED. When the owner runs `watch` "in a few minutes" as told, t - CREATED is already at least 300. The first poll that shows GONE ends the attempt, the purge and close follow, and spot_start creates in zone 1. This is the exact case the implementer's guard was added for: a late-appearing VM gives two VMs, one of them unrecorded and bounded only by its max-run-duration. It is likely rare, because GCE normally lists an accepted insert at once, but the guard does not cover the case it claims to.
findings.fix: Save the time of the last create sent (for example CREATE_SENT, written just before each create at line 325). Time the 5-minute rule in spot_poll from that, and also require two empty listings at least 5 minutes after it.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the guard is timed from when the create was sent (CREATE_SENT) and needs two empty listings after that.

findings.line: 342 (refusal check lists instances only), 347-353 (row closed at zero)
findings.title: After a refused create, only instances are listed: a leftover disk is not seen and the row is closed at zero
findings.detail: A refusal goes on to the next zone, and the all-zones-refused path closes the row at zero, after an empty INSTANCE listing only. If a refused insert leaves the data or boot disk behind (each `--create-disk` is part of the request), the disk bills while no ledger row is open. That breaks claim (2), 'no VM or disk without an open ledger row'. The next spot_start, 10 minutes later, lists disks and dies with 'a disk exists... run teardown', so the watch stalls until the owner acts. The money involved is small.
findings.fix: In the refusal test on line 342 also require `compute disks list` to succeed and be empty. Before close_run ... zero on the no-capacity path, call spot_purge (it verifies both listings); if it is not verified, keep the row open and stop.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: after a refused create both the instance and the disk listing must succeed and be empty before another zone is tried.

findings.title: Taking over a stale lock is check-then-act: two commands can both end up holding it
findings.detail: Sequence: a stale lock is left by a dead pid (for example after a power loss). Command A reads the pid, finds it dead, and is delayed before line 154. Command B reads the dead pid, moves the old lock away, mkdirs a new one and writes its pid. A then runs `mv $SPOT_LOCK $SPOT_LOCK.stale.$$`, which moves B's live lock away, removes it, and mkdirs its own; both now act. I reproduced this in scratch with an instrumented copy of spot_lock that adds a 1 s sleep after the read: both processes printed GOT (rev3A/lockt2.sh). Without the delay, 40 trials of three concurrent takers never doubled up. Once both owners hit an empty pid file (owner killed between mkdir and echo), they sit in the same 3 x 1 s retry loop and reach the takeover together. That widens the window.
findings.fix: Take over by atomic rename and re-check: `mv lock lock.stale.$$`, then confirm that the moved directory's pid file still holds the dead pid you read. If it does not, put it back or refuse. Simpler: create the lock with a unique temp dir and `mv -n` / `ln -s` of the pid as the lock, so the stale check and the claim are one atomic step.
findings.what_was_done: Superseded: after a further finding the directory lock was replaced by a lock the kernel holds on a file (flock), which has no stale state and no take-over.

findings.title: After the Mac restarts, a reused pid makes every Spot command refuse and tells the owner to kill an unrelated process
findings.detail: The lock directory lives in the work dir and survives a power loss or a reboot. kill -0 only tests that some process with that pid exists and belongs to the user. After a reboot the pid can belong to any of the user's processes. watch/teardown then refuse with "stop that command first (... kill PID)", inviting the owner to kill an unrelated process, and the run stalls until the lock is removed by hand.
findings.fix: Store the command and the process start time (`ps -o lstart= -p PID`) in the lock. Treat the lock as live only if `ps -o command= -p PID` contains pilot_local.sh and the start time matches. Otherwise take it over.
findings.what_was_done: Superseded by the same change: nothing is decided from a process number any more.

findings.title: When the 90 % parts rule blocks every zone, the pause says the cap is too small
findings.detail: spot_size returns -1 for an out-of-region zone once PARTS_BYTES passes 90 % of the limit. spot_start then prints "the cap leaves room for an attempt of only -1 s". If no zone in GCP_ZONES is in the bucket's region, it pauses with SPOT_WHY "the cap leaves room for an attempt of only -1 s in the best zone". The owner is pointed at raising the cap, which adds spending authority without fixing anything. The real fix is an in-region zone or a larger GCP_SPOT_PARTS_MAX_GIB.
findings.fix: Have spot_size print a reason word (cap / parts / giveup) with m, and make the per-zone line and SPOT_WHY say "the checkpoint parts (N GiB) are above 90 % of GCP_SPOT_PARTS_MAX_GIB; no attempt may start outside the bucket's region $BUCKET_REGION".
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: sizing gives the reason (cap, give-up time, parts), and the pause for the parts limit names the two remedies and says that raising the cap does not help.

findings.title: Every guest PAUSED starts another paid attempt, including the new pauses that are not deadlines
findings.detail: The SPEC's guest PAUSED meant 'this attempt's deadline'. The fix round added guest pauses for other reasons: transport trouble on restore (G3), 'a state exists that the controller did not see' (G5.2), a failed axiom-summary fetch (G5.6), a killed check (G5.7), and the K1 parts limit. spot_poll treats them all as 'attempt over' and the watch loop starts the next attempt at once. For G5.2 and K1 the next attempt hits the same condition. Each one pays startup and restore (and transfer out of region) until NOPROGRESS reaches 3. That is up to three wasted attempts and a pause whose message ('3 attempts in a row saved no progress') hides the guest's reason.
findings.fix: Have the guest's pause carry a kind (for example `"pause": "deadline"` in status.json or state.json). In spot_poll, only a deadline pause goes on to the next attempt; any other kind ends with spot_pause and the guest's message.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the guest says what kind of pause it is (deadline, retry, parts-limit, stop); only the first two start another attempt unconditionally.

findings.title: The cap test leaves out the inputs each out-of-region attempt downloads
findings.detail: Every attempt fetches inputs/lean.tar.gz, rhv_tools.tar.gz and sampler.py from the bucket (full_guest.sh about lines 1177-1184). Out of region that is a cross-region transfer every attempt (the tarball is the 14-part source archive). Neither XWORST nor the transfer row counts it, and GCP_SPOT_RESERVE_USD is documented as being for checkpoint storage. With 24 attempts out of region the unrecorded transfer adds up to multiples of the tarball size x 0.02 USD/GiB.
findings.fix: Measure the inputs' size at launch (`storage du`), add it to XWORST and to the transfer row of every out-of-region attempt. Or say in config.example.env that the reserve must cover it, and size the default from the measured size.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the size of the inputs is measured at launch and counted in the worst-case transfer and in each transfer row.

verifiers.subject: the guest (cloud/gcp/full_guest.sh), the checkpoint helper (scripts/spot_checkpoint.sh) and their tests
verifiers.summary: Review of the Spot path of the guest and helper: cloud/gcp/full_guest.sh, scripts/spot_checkpoint.sh and the two dev tests. Both tests pass. G1-G4 and most of G5, K1, K4 and K5 hold on the guest side: cross-machine records are written only after a confirm, every fetch is checked, cover is sound, and the ordering of parts, manifest and state is safe. I found no blocker. The old (non-Spot) path is not changed by anything I traced. Two problems are major. First, the setup steps that use the network run again on every attempt, so one transient network failure on a later attempt ends the whole run with a final FAIL. Second, the failed-job count and the lake logs of an attempt that is cut without notice are lost, so the build evidence is weaker than an uninterrupted run's. A third major finding is a test gap: no test runs a cut against the restored done list after a real post-restore Lake build, so a Lake rewrite that changes only mtimes (giving exit 4 and a final FAIL) is never exercised. The rest are minor: a busy loop in the watcher, trim following symlinks, c2 time boxes that cannot fit a short attempt, unconfirmed per-attempt copies, rc 99 pausing every attempt, and a racy root read of /tmp/smoke.log.
verifiers.tests_run: bash scripts/dev/test_spot_checkpoint.sh: last lines "PASS toy: after a source change recompiles saved modules, the next cut says so (status 4)" / "69 cases, 0 failed" (rc 0). TMPDIR=<scratch> bash scripts/dev/test_spot_guest.sh: last lines "PASS 10. axiom-check summaries saved with a checksum and recorded only after a confirm (4 checks, 12 s)" / "13 cases, 0 failed (147 s)" (rc 0).

findings.title: A transient network failure in setup on any later attempt is a final FAIL for the whole run
findings.detail: Every Spot attempt runs the setup t_steps again on a fresh VM: packages (apt), elan (curl from GitHub), source (gcs_get, fetch_checked) and mathlib_cache (lake exe cache get). Any failure calls `finish FAIL`. spot_not_final (lines 507-518) treats an ordinary FAIL as final, and the launcher stops on FAIL status. Sequence: attempt 7 of a run that is 80% done starts; the apt mirror or GitHub returns a 5xx for a minute; t_step elan fails; finish FAIL; the launcher records the run as failed and all the paid-for progress is abandoned. An uninterrupted run is exposed to this only once, but Spot is exposed once per attempt, and that is exactly what Spot was meant to tolerate.
findings.fix: In Spot mode, route failures of the network steps (packages, elan, mathlib_cache, and the source fetch when the cause is transport rather than a checksum mismatch) to spot_pause with a reason such as SETUP_NET, so the launcher retries them under the no-progress limit. Keep checksum or seal mismatches final (touch FAIL_IS_FINAL).
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: in a Spot run a failure of the packages, elan, source or Mathlib-cache step pauses the attempt (retry) and does not end the run; the no-progress rule bounds repeats.

findings.title: failed_job_lines and lake logs of an attempt cut without notice are lost
findings.detail: failed_job_lines is written to state only by spot_record, spot_pause and the final path. spot_apply_pending's state update at line 726 records only parts-modules and TIMEBOX_USED. The lake logs are uploaded only by put_logs on pause or finish. Sequence: attempt 3 builds for 70 minutes, and Lake reports 2 failed jobs that are retried and later succeed; parts are applied every round; the VM is reclaimed with no notice (or the watcher misses the notice), so spot_pause never runs. Attempt 3's failed-job count and logs are gone, c1_build.failed_job_lines_in_all_logs undercounts compared with an uninterrupted run, and the build log evidence for those modules is missing.
findings.fix: Add `--attempt-set-json failed_job_lines=$(failed_lines)` to the state update in spot_apply_pending, and in each part round upload a gzip of the current lake logs to the per-attempt RES/ckpt prefix before the state write, so the record follows the same part, manifest, state order.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the count of failed job lines goes into the state with every part, and the build logs are uploaded with every part.

findings.title: No test runs a cut with the restored done list after a real post-restore Lake build
findings.detail: The toy test checks only that the post-restore lake build left each restored file's sha256 unchanged. cut's done tracking is keyed on (path, size, int mtime), and exit 4 means a saved module was compiled again. If Lake rewrites a restored .olean, .ilean or .trace with identical bytes but a new mtime (for example because it re-hashes a trace or touches outputs), the next cut on the real run exits 4 and the run FAILs final before the seal. The sha-only check cannot see this, and test_spot_guest.sh stubs Lake, so neither test exercises what the restore-resume claim depends on.
findings.fix: Add a toy case: cut, restore into a clean tree, run lake build, then cut again with the restored done list. Expect rc 3 (nothing new) and compare size+mtime as well as sha. If Lake does touch mtimes, make cut compare sha for done entries whose mtime changed before reporting status 4.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the test now builds on a restored tree and cuts again; on this toolchain the build tool changed no restored file. The helper also records each saved file's SHA-256 and treats a file written again with the same bytes as saved again, not as compiled again.

findings.title: Preemption watcher spins without sleeping when the ETag is unusable
findings.detail: spot_watch_preempted clears etag when it contains characters outside [0-9A-Za-z] and sleeps only when the value v is empty. If the metadata server returns a value with a quoted or otherwise unusable ETag, every request returns at once without wait_for_change, and the loop issues requests continuously. That burns a CPU core during the build and floods the metadata server, which can throttle it and delay the real notice.
findings.fix: Sleep 5 s whenever etag is empty after a read, regardless of v, and log once that wait_for_change is not in use.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the watcher sleeps whenever it has no usable ETag.

findings.title: trim opens with rb+ and follows a symbolic link
findings.detail: trim uses open(p, 'rb+'), which follows symlinks. Root calls it on files that safe_cp copied out of the build user's tree (full_guest.sh lines 785 and 805). If the build user swaps the file for a symlink between the plain-file check and the cp, root can truncate or upload the link target. The build user is semi-trusted (it runs project code), so this is a privilege-crossing write.
findings.fix: In trim, open with os.open(p, os.O_RDWR | os.O_NOFOLLOW) and fstat to reject anything that is not a regular file. In safe_cp, copy from an fd opened with O_NOFOLLOW instead of check-then-cp.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: trim refuses anything but a regular file and never follows a link.

findings.title: In Spot, c2 always uses t=C2_TIMEOUT (7200 s), even when the attempt cannot fit it
findings.detail: Spot forces the c2 time box to C2_TIMEOUT=7200. The launcher's minimum attempt length is 5400 s for full-spot (DL about 75 min after DMARGIN). An attempt that starts a c2 unit with less than 7200+FINAL_RESERVE s left is cut at the deadline every time and makes no progress, until NOPROGRESS stops the run, and the money for those attempts is spent with nothing to show.
findings.fix: Before starting a c2 unit, pause with reason NO_ROOM when its time box exceeds left-FINAL_RESERVE, and have the launcher grow the next attempt's length (or refuse a SPOT_MIN below C2_TIMEOUT+FINAL_RESERVE+setup).
findings.what_was_done: Left by decision: in a Spot run the axiom check keeps its full time box; an attempt too short for it is bounded by the no-progress rule and by the cap.

findings.title: Unconfirmed per-attempt copies of c2 and c3 verdicts are uploaded
findings.detail: run_c2 uploads $RES/c2/*.json before any confirm. sync_big uploads c3/results.tsv.gz every 10 minutes, c3_summary writes summary.json before spot_unit_confirmed, and RT/facts.json is written on pause and checkpoint. The cross-machine CK records follow a confirm (G1), but these per-attempt objects can hold verdicts from a machine whose build user was later sighted. A reader of the per-attempt prefix could take them as evidence.
findings.fix: Write the unconfirmed copies under an explicit unconfirmed/ prefix, or mark them unconfirmed in facts.json, and promote them only after spot_confirmed.
findings.what_was_done: Stated, not changed: files under attempt-N/ are that machine's working copies; facts.json and docs/cloud-notes.md section 10.2 say that only what the state records, saved after a confirming hash, is carried between machines.

findings.title: rc 99 (no rc file) pauses every attempt
findings.detail: When a step leaves no rc file (for example runuser fails to start), status 99 is treated as pause-worthy. If the cause is deterministic, such as a broken user setup, every attempt pauses at the same point and the run spends attempts until NOPROGRESS stops it.
findings.fix: Count consecutive rc-99 pauses at the same step in state and make the second one final with a clear HARD_FAIL_MSG.
findings.what_was_done: Left by decision: bounded by the no-progress rule at three attempts.

findings.title: Root reads the build user's /tmp/smoke.log with a plain check that can race
findings.detail: spot_ckpt_final calls built_in_log /tmp/smoke.log. The file is checked as plain and then read as root. The build user can swap it for a FIFO between the check and the read, so the final checkpoint hangs until the deadline.
findings.fix: Open it with O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK, fstat to confirm a regular file, and read from that fd. Or copy it with the same safe copy used for parts.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: root reads the smoke log only from a copy of its own, made with a time limit.

items_checked.note: The cross-machine CK uploads (results, c2 json, unit records) all follow spot_confirm (lines 593-634; results round lines 781-795; c2_save lines 1077-1087). Only the unconfirmed per-attempt copies remain (line 1563, sync_big, summary.json, RT/facts.json); see the minor finding.

Root no longer reads paths the pilot controls without a check: cut uses --out - (line 658ff) and restore uses check_member/O_NOFOLLOW. One leftover is the racy read of /tmp/smoke.log at line 753 (minor).

verifiers.subject: the launcher (cloud/gcp/pilot_local.sh) and its test
verifiers.summary:
I checked the launcher (cloud/gcp/pilot_local.sh), its test script and config.example.env against FIXES3.md items A15 to A25 and the launcher side of K7. My own run of the test, with the default TMPDIR, ended with these five lines:
"PASS old_mode_full" / "PASS old_full_edges" / "PASS spot_vm_matches_on_demand" / "65 passed, 0 failed" / "rc=0".

What holds up:
- Durable start (A15): I found no path on which a create is sent before the row and the state naming the attempt are on disk. The only create is at line 434. In both the first zone and every later one it is preceded by `spot_sync "$LEDGER"` (line 421, once per attempt) and by a state save plus `spot_sync "$STATE"` (lines 425-426).
- Pause kinds: they are read in both spot_poll and spot_account, only from the current attempt's status. They survive a stop between accounting and acting, and they survive a teardown.
- PARTS_FULL never blocks a zone in the bucket's region.
- Old modes: every hunk they run is the same as HEAD except close_run, which now writes through a temporary file, syncs it and keeps the file mode. Its output stays byte-identical in the tests.
- Bash 3.2 and BSD tools: everything new is compatible. F_FULLFSYNC on a directory works on APFS (scratch and <REDACTED> are both APFS).

What I refuted:
1. Lock: two commands can hold it at the same time. I reproduced this with the real lock functions taken out of the file and sleeps added only to widen the windows (rev5a/race/inject.sh); without the sleeps, 30 rounds of 4 takers each showed no overlap.
2. A rehearsal can exit 0 with a cut that was really done by deleting the VM, not by Google's reclaim.
Both are major. I also found several minor issues; they are listed below.
verifiers.tests_run:
Ran `cd <REPO> && /bin/bash scripts/dev/test_spot_launcher.sh` with the default TMPDIR. Log: <SCRATCH>/spotdesign/rev5a/test.log. Last five lines, exactly as printed:
PASS old_mode_full
PASS old_full_edges
PASS spot_vm_matches_on_demand
65 passed, 0 failed
rc=0

Experiments, all in scratch (no repository file changed):
(1) rev5a/race/build.sh takes the real spot_lstart, spot_lock_live, spot_lock and spot_unlock out of the file into a script named pilot_local.sh. It ran 30 rounds of 4 concurrent takers of a stale lock (dead pid), with no overlap: 21 rounds had 3 serial acquisitions and 9 had 2, and every other taker died correctly.
(2) rev5a/race/inject.sh is the same code with sleeps added only to widen its windows (S1 before the rename, S2 after it, S3 after mkdir). It showed A's lstart and pid writes failing while B had the fresh lock moved away, B dying, and C later taking over A's lock while A held it. The result was OVERLAP plus BADPID: two holders.
(3) F_FULLFSYNC and fsync on a directory file descriptor in the APFS scratch directory: both succeed.

findings.title: Lock takeover can still leave two holders: the new holder never checks that its own writes landed
findings.detail: Sequence: a stale lock L0 holds a dead pid P. Commands A and B both read P (line 187), and both find it not live (189). A renames L0 away (195), finds it is the lock it examined, removes it (202) and makes a fresh lock L1 with mkdir (186). B now runs its own rename at 195. That rename succeeds, but it moves A's fresh L1 to $SPOT_LOCK.stale.B. B reads pid2, which is empty or A's pid and so is not P; it moves L1 back (198) and dies, as designed. Meanwhile A runs line 208 (`spot_lstart > $SPOT_LOCK/lstart`) and line 209 (`echo $$ > $SPOT_LOCK/pid.tmp && mv`). These fail with 'No such file or directory' while L1 is moved away, and A carries on with SPOT_LOCKED=1. The lock directory is then back in place, but empty. Any later command, such as a teardown or a second watch, finds an empty pid, waits 3 x 1 s (188), treats the lock as stale (spot_lock_live returns 1 for an empty pid) and takes it over while A, a watch that runs for hours, is still alive. Two Spot commands then run at once, which is what the lock exists to prevent: two watches can each pass spot_start's empty-project check. When A exits, spot_unlock (212) also removes the other command's lock. A third taker can produce the same result directly: C runs mkdir in the moment B has L1 moved away, B then does not move it back (198), and A and C both hold. Reproduced with the real functions and widened windows (rev5a/race/inject.sh). Output: A's errors are 'state.lock/lstart: No such file or directory' and 'state.lock/pid.tmp: No such file or directory'; B dies; C prints 'taking over the lock left by 'unknown''; the overlap file shows 'OVERLAP 1014' and 'BADPID 735 lockpid='. The natural windows are a single ps call and a single rename wide, so this needs near-simultaneous commands. The test case lock_race (two takers, six times) cannot exercise it.
findings.fix: Make the lock appear complete in one step. Write pid, lstart and command into a private directory $SPOT_LOCK.new.$$, then publish it with a rename that fails if the target exists (python os.rename onto a missing path; BSD `mv dir existing_dir` nests the directory instead of failing, so do not rely on mv). As a minimum, after line 209 re-read $SPOT_LOCK/pid and $SPOT_LOCK/lstart and go round the loop again unless both are this process's. Make spot_unlock remove the lock only if its pid is still $$.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed by replacing the lock: one the kernel holds on a file (flock on a descriptor the command keeps open), released when the command ends however it ends. Tried by the lead and by the next verifier: many takers at once, exactly one holder every time.

findings.title: A simulated reclaim that Google accepted but that never took effect is reported 'done as configured', so the rehearsal can exit 0
findings.detail: Sequence for the cut build:simulate. spot_poll records CUTS_DONE="build:simulate" (line 637). `instances simulate-maintenance-event --async` returns 0, so cut_at is set (648). Then nothing happens: the VM stays RUNNING and the guest never reports RECLAIMED. Five minutes later line 630 ends the attempt with 'the VM was still there 5 minutes after the simulated reclaim', and spot_account's spot_purge deletes the VM. The real cut was therefore a delete, but CUTS_DONE never gains '>delete'. spot_cuts_report (779) prints 'build:simulate: done as configured', SPOT_CUTS_MISSED stays 0, and spot_finish leaves SPOT_RC=0. This is the exact case A16 is meant to catch: whether Google's forced reclaim, and the guest's handling of it, really happen on a real machine is only known from a paid rehearsal. No test covers it; rehearsal_simulate_refused covers only a refused simulate.
findings.fix: At line 630 add `CUTS_DONE="$CUTS_DONE>delete"; spot_save` before returning (the CUTS_DONE entry for the item made at 637 is the last word). Add a test whose fake accepts the simulate and leaves the VM RUNNING; it must expect 'done by fallback (delete)' and exit 4.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: an accepted simulate whose machine is still there five minutes later is recorded as done by fallback (exit status 4); later made to survive a restarted watch.

findings.title: A cut is recorded as done before it is sent; an interruption in between makes the report say 'done as configured'
findings.detail: Line 637 saves CUTS_DONE and CUT_ATTEMPT before the gcloud reset, simulate or delete is sent (by design, 'never cut twice'). Sequence: Ctrl-C (the INT trap exits 130) or a crash while `gcloud compute instances reset` is running, or for a delete cut before poll returns. The next watch sees CUT_ATTEMPT=ATTEMPT and the item in CUTS_DONE, so it never makes the cut, watches the attempt to its natural end, and the report says 'done as configured'. The run exits 0.
findings.fix: Record a marker such as '>pending' at 637, and replace it with the final form only after the call has returned. spot_cuts_report should count a pending item as NOT DONE.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: a cut is recorded as pending before its command is sent and given its final form only afterwards; pending counts as NOT DONE.

findings.title: A failed read of status.json at accounting time loses the pause kind of an attempt that ended unwatched
findings.detail: On the 'found ended' path (line 873), SPOT_PKIND was reset at line 864. If `storage cat status.json` fails transiently at line 711, spot_pause_read is never called, PKIND is saved as empty (743), and the watch loop treats the attempt as a deadline. A 'stop' therefore leads to one more paid attempt that will end the same way. A 'parts-limit' is lost too: PARTS_FULL is not set, so an out-of-region attempt can start whenever the parts are under the 90 % rule, and it will pause again. The money stays within the cap. On the watched path the poll's kind survives a failed re-read, but a successful re-read always overrides it. So if the guest's last write is a later PAUSED with no kind (for example from its watchdog), a 'stop' that the poll saw becomes 'deadline'.
findings.fix: In spot_account, treat a failed status fetch as an accounting failure (exit 1, row already closed, rerun watch), as is done for the checkpoints at 719-721. Keep the poll's kind when the re-read gives a less cautious one.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: a failed read of the status at accounting time is an accounting failure (run watch again), and the kind of a pause is never weakened.

findings.title: The 25-minute 'reported nothing' rule and the local deadline still count from CREATED, not CREATE_SENT
findings.detail: A17 moved only the not-listed guard to CREATE_SENT. Sequence: earlier zones refuse slowly, then the create in a later zone is sent at CREATED+D. The guest of that VM is killed after only 1500-D seconds with no report (three absent polls). spot_account then purges a booting VM and counts an attempt without progress. Likewise ldl=CREATED+MAXRUN+300 makes the watcher delete the VM early when D > 300. No money is lost; work is lost.
findings.fix: Use $sent (CREATE_SENT, falling back to CREATED) in both places.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: both clocks count from when the create was sent.

findings.title: The STARTING=N save is not synced before the row is; a power cut there makes a later watch charge a phantom attempt
findings.detail: Line 417's spot_save, a rename, is not synced, while the row at 420 is (421). Sequence: power cut after 421 and before 426. On reboot the ledger durably holds attempt N's open row, but the state may be the old one: ATTEMPT=N-1, STARTING empty, accounted. watch then sees an open row for RUNTAG and 'watches attempt N-1'. Once the VM is GONE (LAST_SEEN of N-1 is set) it accounts and closes attempt N's row with seconds = now - row time, capped at the old MAXRUN+120. No VM ever existed, so that is up to MAXRUN of phantom spend counted against the cap. This errs on the safe side but can pause the run on the cap. The contract's wording requires the sync only at (b), so this is the contract's order, not a deviation from it.
findings.fix: Call spot_sync "$STATE" after the save at 417 (once per attempt), so that the attempt is named on disk before its row exists.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the state that names the attempt is forced to disk before its row is appended.

findings.title: PARTS_FULL stores the limit in force at handling time, not the limit the attempt was given (the implementer's own note, confirmed)
findings.detail: Sequence: an attempt runs with full-parts-max-bytes=60 GiB. The owner raises GCP_SPOT_PARTS_MAX_GIB to 80 while it runs, and the guest pauses with parts-limit. The watch sets PARTS_FULL to 80 GiB in bytes, so the remedy already applied counts for nothing. With no zone in the bucket's region, the run pauses telling the owner to raise the limit, which they already did; they must raise it past 80.
findings.fix: Store the PARTS_MAX_BYTES sent in the attempt's metadata in a state key at create time (for example ATT_PMAX, saved with CREATE_SENT), and set PARTS_FULL from it.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the parts limit actually given to the attempt is stored and used.

findings.title: The failure path of the state sync (lines 426-428) is untested
findings.detail: durable_sync_fails makes the first sync fail, which is the ledger's (421). The branch that puts STARTING=N back after a failed state sync, both with issued=0 and with issued=1, is never run. The check at 1193-1205 also cannot tell a sync made by spot_sync from one made by close_run or spot_ledger_zone; it works only because it orders by path and by CREATE lines.
findings.fix: Add a case where only the state's sync fails (for example, the python wrapper fails when argv names the state file). It must assert no create, STARTING=N in the state, and that the next watch closes the row at zero.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: a test fails the state's own sync and checks that no create is sent.

items_checked.note: The ledger is synced after the row (421) and the state is synced before every create (425-426), including later zones. close_run and spot_ledger_zone sync the file and its folder; the transfer row is synced (734, warning only). A failed sync dies before the create. The STARTING=N save at 417 is not synced (minor finding).

The report is called from spot_finish (before rm), spot_pause and abandon. cuts.txt is written and mirrored. SPOT_RC=4 reaches the exit through spot_watch and caffeinate's exec. A simulate that was accepted but never took effect is reported as done as configured (major finding), and a cut interrupted right after it was recorded is reported as done (minor).
Lines 589-620 need 300 s since CREATE_SENT (or CREATED) and two GONE listings in a row. The 25-minute rule and the local deadline still use CREATED (minor).
Line 448 requires the instances and disks listings to succeed and be empty; otherwise spot_create_unclear.

items_checked.note: Start time and command liveness checks are correct, and TZ=UTC0 is a sound deviation. The rename takeover is not race-free: the new holder's writes can fail unnoticed, and the lock is then taken over while held. Reproduced (major finding).

Both rewrites resolve realpath, put the temporary file in the target's folder and chmod it to the old mode before os.replace. The old-mode test checks mode 640.

The kind is read in poll and in account, only for this attempt; no kind counts as deadline; it is kept in PKIND/PMSG across a stop and a teardown. stop pauses with the contract's sentence; parts-limit sets PARTS_FULL, which is cleared by a larger limit; an unknown kind pauses. The hunks the old modes run are the dispatcher guards (spot_state_exists checks, which are false for an old state) and close_run (same bytes written; now atomic, synced and keeping the mode). In spot_apply_pending, after the manifest upload (749), the move of pending.list into done.txt and the move of manifest.new into manifest.tsv (751), and the rm of the pending files (754), the round now runs spot_lake_n and spot_put_lake_logs (760-761). findings.title: A delete cut that never happened is reported 'done as configured', exit 0
findings.detail: A delete cut is written to CUTS_DONE in its final form ('seal:delete') and CUT_ATTEMPT=ATTEMPT is saved before anything is deleted. The poll then returns and the delete happens later, in spot_account -> spot_purge. If the watch ends before the delete request is sent, a later watch does NOT delete the VM. Ways it can end there: spot_purge cannot list for 10 minutes and exits 1 (line 489), Ctrl-C lands during the purge's first `instances list`, or a kill -9. The ledger row is still open, so spot_watch (line 887) calls spot_poll again. spot_poll has no memory that a delete was decided, and it makes no further cut because CUT_ATTEMPT==ATTEMPT (line 631). The attempt therefore runs to its natural end, and spot_cuts_report prints 'seal:delete: done as configured'. The run exits 0 although no attempt was ever cut at seal, so a resume after a seal cut was never exercised. The implementer's reason ('its open row makes every later watch or teardown delete the VM') is true for teardown but false for watch. Reproduced in <SCRATCH>/spotdesign/rev6a/exp/exp.sh, case e1, with the real harness. Settings: GCP_SPOT_REHEARSAL_CUTS=seal:delete, and the purge's two listings made to fail 100 times. Result: watch1 exit 1 with CUTS_DONE=[seal:delete] CUT_ATTEMPT=1 and the VM still listed; failures cleared; watch2 exit 0, 'attempt 1 is over: the guest reported DONE', 'seal:delete: done as configured', creates: 1, deaths: [(1,'deleted',3000)].
findings.fix: Record delete as '<item>>pending' like the other cuts. Give it its final form '<item>' only after spot_purge has verified the VM gone, in spot_account when CUT_ATTEMPT==ATTEMPT. Alternatively, at the start of spot_poll, end the attempt at once (SPOT_END=over) when a delete cut is recorded for this attempt. Add a test: purge fails after a delete cut, the next watch must not keep polling, and the result is exit 4 or a real delete.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: a delete cut stays pending until the purge has verified that nothing is left, and a watch that starts again with a delete pending ends the attempt at once.

findings.title: A simulated reclaim with no effect is 'done as configured', exit 0, if the watch restarts within 5 minutes
findings.detail: When `simulate-maintenance-event --async` is accepted, spot_cut_set writes '<item>' (final) at once. cut_at and cut_item exist only in local variables of spot_poll. If the watch stops within 300 s (Ctrl-C, terminal closed, kill) and is started again, cut_at is empty, so the A27 fallback never triggers. CUT_ATTEMPT==ATTEMPT also blocks any further cut. If Google never acts on the simulate, the attempt runs to its natural end and the report says 'done as configured' with exit 0. The implementer named this as a remaining edge but did not fix it. A27 asks that an accepted simulate with no effect never count as done as configured. Reproduced in exp.sh, case e2: simulate_noop, with stop_watch_at 560 s after launch (the simulate went out at t+400). Result: watch1 exit 130 with CUTS_DONE=[build:simulate]; watch2 exit 0, 'attempt 1 is over: the guest reported DONE', 'build:simulate: done as configured'.

findings.title: teardown and old-mode launch run unlocked while a Spot launch has not yet written its state
findings.detail: `teardown` picks the Spot path only if spot_state_exists (line 1105), and old `launch` refuses only if spot_state_exists (line 956). `launch full-spot` takes the lock at line 840 but writes no state until line 854. In between come several seconds of gcloud and git calls: bucket describe, storage du, commit_ok. Sequence A: terminal 1 runs `launch full-spot`. Terminal 2 runs `teardown` (for example after a refusal message that says to run teardown) in that window. Teardown takes the old path (lines 1106-1136): it finds no state, lists no instances, and 'verifies'. Its `rm -f "$STATE"` (line 1128) can land after spot_start's last spot_save (line 414) while the create is in flight. The VM is then created with an open row and no state. Every later `watch` says 'no run state found'. An old teardown deletes the VM but cannot close the row, because RUNTAG is empty (line 1127). The row stays open for good, its cost is never written to the ledger, and every launch is blocked until the ledger is edited by hand. Sequence B: `launch full` in that window passes the check at line 959 and the instance list at line 960, as spot_start's checks at lines 372-382 do. Both create a VM: two VMs at once. Old modes take no lock by decision, and two old launches could already race at HEAD, so I rate this major rather than blocker. It is still a path on which a command acting on a Spot run runs without the lock.
findings.fix: Without creating anything, make `teardown` and old-mode `launch` probe the lock before choosing a path, when $SPOT_LOCK exists: open it with `exec 9<` and try flock LOCK_NB in python. If it is held, refuse with the same sentence. When no lock file exists, the old-mode bytes and behaviour stay as now. Another option: write a minimal SPOT='1' state immediately after spot_lock in spot_launch, and remove it on every refusal path.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: a Spot launch writes its state at once after taking the lock, the old-path teardown never removes a Spot run's state, and old-mode launch and teardown take the lock whenever the lock file exists.

findings.title: 'up to a minute' understates how long an orphaned gcloud child keeps the lock, and the message names a dead process
findings.detail: After a kill -9 of a watch or teardown, any gcloud child that inherited descriptor 9 keeps the lock until it exits. That includes `instances delete` (which waits for the operation), `instances create` and `storage cp -r`. Such calls commonly take 1 to 3 minutes and can hang with no timeout when the API stalls. My tests confirmed that a child holding descriptor 9 keeps the lock (take.sh in raw mode) and that spot_sleep does not. Meanwhile the refusal names the dead bash's process number from .info and says to kill it. That process is gone, and its number may have been reused by an unrelated process.
findings.fix: Check whether the named process is alive (kill -0). If it is not, say that a child of it (gcloud) still holds the lock and how to find it: `lsof <lock file>`. Drop 'up to a minute', or change it to 'a few minutes'.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: the refusal says when the named command has ended and a child of it still holds the lock, and no longer says "up to a minute".

findings.title: A stalled log upload now delays the manifest by up to about 12 minutes per log
findings.detail:
The contract asked for the order part, logs, manifest. A log upload that fails costs nothing: I checked that it stays a WARNING and the round goes on. A log upload that stalls is different. gz_put calls gcs_put, which makes 5 tries; each try can take up to 20 s to connect plus 120 s below 1 KB/s, and the waits between tries add 75 s. That is roughly 12 to 13 minutes per log, and every log of the attempt goes up in each round.

Sequence:
1. spot_ckpt_round uploads part-N.
2. spot_put_lake_logs starts on lake_build_1.log, and the network stalls.
3. For up to about 12 minutes, part-N is in the bucket but in no manifest.
4. If Google reclaims the machine in that window, part-N is lost and its modules are compiled again by the next attempt.
5. In spot_pause after the deadline, the same wait sits before the last manifest. The watchdog's 600 s + 1800 s usually covers it.

No evidence is wrong; only compute is lost.
findings.fix: Bound the log uploads inside a part round, for example with one try, or `timeout 120` around each gz_put in spot_put_lake_logs. Or, in pause mode, upload the logs after the state write (put_logs runs later in spot_pause anyway).
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: inside a part round each log gets one upload attempt with a limit of two minutes.

findings.title: The RECLAIMED state writes do not carry the saved work
findings.detail:
The contract says "every state write that ends an attempt carry the saved work", then names spot_pause. Two writes that end an attempt do not pass --parts-modules or TIMEBOX_USED:
- spot_reclaimed (line 597): `--attempt-set ended=RECLAIMED`
- the preemption watcher (line 620): the same write

Sequence:
1. The part loop is in spot_apply_pending: it has uploaded the manifest and moved it into place locally.
2. Google's notice arrives. spot_reclaimed kills the loop before its spot_state runs.
3. The watcher's or spot_reclaimed's RECLAIMED write leaves parts_modules and progress at the old values.
4. The launcher accounts that attempt as making no progress (test_spot_launcher: "RECLAIMED before any new checkpoint counts as no progress"), which brings the run one step closer to its no-progress limit.
5. The next attempt's first state write recounts the manifest and so corrects it.

The implementer disclosed this.
findings.fix: Add `--parts-modules "$(awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 {s += $5} END {print s + 0}' "$SPD/manifest.tsv" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)"` to both RECLAIMED writes. It is one awk, and fast enough for the reclaim path.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: both writes that record a reclaim carry the saved work.

findings.title: A saved file with an mtime in the future is put off at every round until the last cut
findings.detail:
The deferral test is `lstat(...).st_mtime >= settle`. With true mtimes, a changed file is judged in the next round, 600 s later. But the build user owns these files and can set their times (for example with `touch -d 2100-01-01`), and a clock step can do the same.

Sequence:
1. A saved .olean is rewritten with other bytes and given an mtime in the future.
2. Every loop cut puts it off: "1 saved files changed in the last seconds; looked at again next round".
3. The pause cut (settle = t) puts it off too.
4. Only the final cut (`--all`, strict, so status 4) or the next attempt's restored-compiled-again check sees it.

No wrong result can pass this way. It only delays when the run ends, and loop rounds keep cutting other modules meanwhile.
findings.fix: Put a file off only if its mtime is at or after settle and not more than a little ahead of the current time, e.g. `settle <= mtime <= time.time() + 60`. A file whose mtime is further in the future would then be judged at once.
findings.what_was_done: Fixed: a saved file whose time is more than a minute in the future is judged at once.

findings.title: First-ever Spot launch can still race an old-path teardown or an old-mode launch (no lock file yet)
findings.detail:
Teardown race. Old-path teardown runs line 1145: spot_state_exists is false. It then runs line 1146: $SPOT_LOCK does not exist yet, so it takes no lock. In the gap before line 1147, the first-ever `launch full-spot` creates the lock file, takes the lock and early-saves its state (line 885). Teardown then sources that Spot state at line 1147, so RUNTAG and MAXRUN are the Spot run's. It lists the instances and verifies the project empty, because the attempt's create is still in flight. At line 1168 it runs close_run on the Spot run's row, which spot_start opened at line 421. Line 1169 keeps the state. The create then succeeds: a Spot VM runs with its ledger row already closed at about 0 s. If nobody watches, that money is not in the ledger until Google deletes the VM at MAXRUN. If watch is run, the purge in spot_account (found-ended path) deletes the VM, but the row is still not re-closed. I reproduced the consequence in a scratch copy of the launcher, with a hook between lines 1146 and 1147 that moves a launched Spot run's state back into place. Teardown deleted lean-full-spot, closed row full-spot#1 at 0 s and printed 'a Spot run was launched meanwhile: its state ... is kept'. The scratch copy is in rev7a/exp/exp2.sh. The window is microseconds wide and exists only before any Spot command has ever run in the work directory.

Launch race. An old-mode `launch` passes lines 995 and 996 just before the same first Spot launch's early save. It appends its own row and writes STATE at line 1052. The Spot launch then refuses at line 385 (a row is open), and spot_refuse at line 379 runs `rm -f STATE`. That removes the old run's state while its VM is being created. Its watch then says 'no run state found', and teardown cannot close its row.
findings.fix: Neither fix changes any case HEAD can meet. In the old-path teardown, after sourcing the state at line 1147: if SPOT is 1, hand over to spot_teardown or die, instead of acting on a Spot run without its lock. In spot_refuse, remove the state only if it is still this launch's own: SPOT is 1 and RUNTAG equals the launch's RUNTAG.
